title: Acute pulmonary embolism: risk stratification and treatment
subject: cardiology
summary: Assess clinical probability, use D-dimer and CT pulmonary angiography, stratify by haemodynamic status, sPESI, RV dysfunction and troponin; give systemic thrombolysis plus UFH for high-risk (shocked) PE, anticoagulation with monitoring for intermediate risk, and early discharge on a DOAC for low risk.

sections.title: Recognise and estimate probability
items: Suspect PE with breathlessness, pleuritic chest pain, haemoptysis, syncope, unexplained tachycardia or hypoxaemia, especially with risk factors (surgery, immobility, cancer, pregnancy or postpartum, oestrogens, previous VTE).

High-risk PE means haemodynamic instability: cardiac arrest, obstructive shock (SBP below 90 mmHg or vasopressors needed, with hypoperfusion), or persistent hypotension (SBP below 90 mmHg or a fall of 40 mmHg or more for over 15 minutes not due to arrhythmia, hypovolaemia or sepsis).

Two-level Wells score: signs of DVT 3, PE the most likely diagnosis 3, heart rate above 100/min 1.5, immobilisation 3 days or more or surgery within 4 weeks 1.5, previous DVT or PE 1.5, haemoptysis 1, active cancer 1. PE likely if above 4, unlikely if 4 or less.

Low clinical probability and all PERC criteria met (age under 50, heart rate under 100/min, SpO2 95% or more, no haemoptysis, no oestrogen use, no previous VTE, no unilateral leg swelling, no surgery or trauma needing hospitalisation within 4 weeks): no further testing.

sections.title: Suspected high-risk PE (shock)
items: Resuscitate: oxygen, cautious fluid (no more than about 500 mL), noradrenaline for hypotension; avoid intubation where possible because induction can precipitate arrest.
Give UFH IV bolus immediately (weight-adjusted) without waiting for imaging.
Bedside echocardiography: RV dilatation with no other cause in an unstable patient justifies reperfusion if CTPA is not immediately possible; confirm with CTPA once stable enough.
Systemic thrombolysis is recommended for high-risk PE. If thrombolysis is contraindicated or has failed: surgical embolectomy or catheter-directed treatment where available.
Cardiac arrest from suspected PE: give thrombolysis during CPR and continue CPR for 60 to 90 minutes after the dose.

sections.title: Diagnostic tests
items: PE unlikely: D-dimer first. Use the age-adjusted cut-off above 50 years (age x 10 mcg/L FEU). A negative D-dimer excludes PE; a positive one leads to CTPA.
PE likely: go straight to CT pulmonary angiography; do not use D-dimer. V/Q scan if contrast is contraindicated (severe CKD, contrast allergy) or in pregnancy with a normal chest X-ray.
Compression ultrasound showing proximal DVT in a patient with suspected PE confirms VTE and is enough to start treatment.
For risk stratification: troponin, BNP or NT-proBNP, echocardiography or CT RV/LV ratio (1.0 or more suggests RV dysfunction), creatinine, CBC, coagulation, and blood gas if hypoxaemic.

sections.title: Risk classes and management
items: sPESI (1 point each): age over 80, cancer, chronic heart failure or chronic lung disease, heart rate 110/min or more, SBP below 100 mmHg, SpO2 below 90%. Score 0 is low risk.

Low risk (sPESI 0 or PESI class I to II, no RV dysfunction, troponin normal if measured): anticoagulate and consider early discharge or home treatment if there are no Hestia exclusions and good social support.
Intermediate-low risk (sPESI 1 or more with RV dysfunction or raised troponin, but not both): anticoagulation in hospital.

Intermediate-high risk (sPESI 1 or more with both RV dysfunction and raised troponin): anticoagulation (LMWH preferred, UFH if reperfusion may be needed) with close monitoring for 48 to 72 hours; rescue thrombolysis if haemodynamic decompensation. Do not give routine full-dose thrombolysis.

Anticoagulant choice: LMWH or fondaparinux preferred over UFH initially in stable patients; DOAC (apixaban or rivaroxaban directly, or dabigatran or edoxaban after at least 5 days of parenteral therapy) preferred over VKA. Use UFH in shock, possible reperfusion, CrCl below 30 mL/min or severe obesity.

Thrombolysis contraindications as for STEMI (prior intracranial haemorrhage, recent ischaemic stroke, CNS tumour, recent major trauma or surgery, active bleeding, bleeding disorder). In high-risk PE, relative contraindications may be accepted given the mortality.

sections.title: Special groups
items: Pregnancy: LMWH by early pregnancy weight throughout pregnancy and at least 6 weeks postpartum (minimum 3 months in total); DOACs and warfarin are not used. High-risk PE in pregnancy is still treated with thrombolysis or embolectomy.
Cancer: edoxaban or rivaroxaban (or apixaban) as alternatives to LMWH; prefer LMWH or apixaban in gastrointestinal or genitourinary cancer with bleeding risk.
Antiphospholipid syndrome (especially triple positive): warfarin, not DOACs.
Severe renal impairment (CrCl below 30 mL/min): UFH then VKA; avoid dabigatran, and use other DOACs only per label.

sections.title: Duration and follow-up
items: Anticoagulate for at least 3 months. Stop after 3 months if PE was provoked by a major transient risk factor (surgery, trauma).
Consider indefinite anticoagulation for unprovoked PE, a persistent risk factor, or recurrence; reduced-dose apixaban (2.5 mg twice daily) or rivaroxaban (10 mg daily) after 6 months is an option.
Review at 3 to 6 months for persistent breathlessness or exercise limitation: echocardiography and V/Q scan to screen for chronic thromboembolic pulmonary hypertension.

sections.title: Pitfalls
items: Using D-dimer in high-probability patients, or a fixed cut-off in elderly patients.
Routine full-dose thrombolysis in stable intermediate-risk PE (more bleeding, including intracranial).
Large fluid boluses in RV failure, and intubating a shocked PE patient without preparing vasopressors.
The 2026 ACC/AHA acute PE guideline uses a different severity classification; this protocol follows the ESC 2019 risk classes.

drugs.name: Alteplase (rtPA)
drugs.dose: 100 mg IV over 2 hours; accelerated regimen 0.6 mg/kg over 15 minutes (maximum 50 mg) in cardiac arrest or imminent arrest
drugs.notes: UFH infusion may continue during alteplase; check aPTT after the infusion.

drugs.name: Streptokinase
drugs.dose: 250 000 IU IV over 30 minutes, then 100 000 IU/h for 12 to 24 hours; accelerated regimen 1.5 million IU over 2 hours
drugs.notes: Stop UFH during the infusion. Hypotension, allergy; do not repeat after previous exposure.

drugs.name: Urokinase
drugs.dose: 4400 IU/kg IV over 10 minutes, then 4400 IU/kg/h for 12 to 24 hours; accelerated regimen 3 million IU over 2 hours

drugs.name: Unfractionated heparin (UFH)
drugs.dose: 80 IU/kg IV bolus, then 18 IU/kg/h infusion, adjusted to aPTT 1.5 to 2.5 times control
drugs.notes: High-risk PE, planned reperfusion, CrCl below 30 mL/min.

drugs.name: Enoxaparin
drugs.dose: 1 mg/kg SC every 12 hours (or 1.5 mg/kg once daily)
drugs.notes: CrCl below 30 mL/min: 1 mg/kg once daily or use UFH. Anti-Xa monitoring in pregnancy, extreme weight or renal impairment.

drugs.name: Apixaban
drugs.dose: 10 mg orally twice daily for 7 days, then 5 mg twice daily; extended phase after 6 months 2.5 mg twice daily
drugs.notes: Can be started without parenteral lead-in.

drugs.name: Rivaroxaban
drugs.dose: 15 mg orally twice daily with food for 21 days, then 20 mg once daily; extended phase after 6 months 10 mg once daily
drugs.notes: Can be started without parenteral lead-in. Avoid if CrCl below 15 mL/min.

drugs.name: Dabigatran or edoxaban
drugs.dose: After at least 5 days of parenteral anticoagulation: dabigatran 150 mg twice daily, or edoxaban 60 mg once daily (30 mg if CrCl 15 to 50 mL/min, weight 60 kg or less, or strong P-gp inhibitor)
drugs.notes: Dabigatran contraindicated if CrCl below 30 mL/min.

drugs.name: Warfarin
drugs.dose: Start with parenteral anticoagulant for at least 5 days and until INR is 2.0 or more for 24 hours; target INR 2.0 to 3.0
drugs.notes: Use in antiphospholipid syndrome, mechanical valves or when DOACs are unsuitable.

sources.title: 2019 ESC Guidelines for the diagnosis and management of acute pulmonary embolism
